get.description: Search stored events in one time window, one page at a time. The window runs from `from` (inclusive) to `to` (exclusive) on the stored `timestamp`: the event's occurredAt, or the time Logbird received it when occurredAt was absent or unusable. Without `from` it is at most the 24 hours before `to` (the store limits, 1900-01-01T00:00:00.000Z to 2299-12-31T23:59:59.999Z, can shorten it); without `to` it ends at the server clock. The response states the window it applied as `range`: a history read here is complete only for that window, whatever `totalExact` says. Events sort by `timestamp`, then by event `id` in the same direction (`order`). Events in the same millisecond are ordered by id, not by cause: read causation from `context.parentEventId`. Follow `nextCursor` until it is null, sending the same `q` and `order`, and the first page's `range` as `from` and `to` (a cursor carries no window, so omitted bounds would be resolved again on every page), and use absolute times in `q`: a relative time (`receivedAt:>now-1h`) is read against each request's clock and can drop an event between pages. Each page continues after the previous page's last event. Fixed bounds keep the window, not the events: the pass is still not a snapshot. Paging is not a snapshot: an event stored after you started, with a `timestamp` behind your position, is not on the later pages. `receivedAt:` in `q` helps find late arrivals, with a `from` early enough to cover when they can have occurred (the window still filters on `timestamp`). Receipt times are not a strict sequence: events can share a millisecond, and an event recovered after a storage failure keeps its original receipt time. So re-read with a generous overlap (`receivedAt:>=` a time well before the last one you saw) and drop ids you already have; an overlap narrows the gap but cannot prove it closed. `total` counts the whole window (a lower bound when `totalExact` is false). A scoped key or viewer token sees only its scope, and `q` cannot widen it. To rebuild a record's whole history step by step, follow the reading guide: https://github.com/joodlab/logbird/blob/master/docs/reading-history.md

parameters.description: Start of the time window, inclusive, on the stored `timestamp`: the event's occurredAt, or the time Logbird received it when occurredAt was absent or unusable (an unusable value is usually noted, cut to 256 characters, in `attributes['logbird.occurredAt.rejected']`; the event detail's `payload` keeps what was sent). Send an ISO 8601 date-time in UTC (Z) or with an offset, read to the millisecond: a date-time without an offset is read in the server's time zone, and a date alone is midnight UTC. The server parses it with JavaScript's Date, so other spellings that Date accepts are read too; they are not portable. Default: `to` minus 24 hours. A bound outside what the store holds is moved onto its limit: `from` no earlier than 1900-01-01T00:00:00.000Z, `to` no later than 2299-12-31T23:59:59.999Z (exclusive, so an event at exactly that last millisecond cannot be read). The window applied is returned as `range` (export: the X-Logbird-Range-From and X-Logbird-Range-To headers).

get.description: One event by id. No time window applies. Returns the event; its original `payload` (null under any field mask); `parents`, its nearest ancestors through `context.parentEventId`, furthest first, at most 100. get.description: How far back this caller's history reaches. `oldestEventAt` is the `timestamp` of the oldest event this caller can find through search: the first event that an `order=asc` search over the widest window (`from` 1900-01-01T00:00:00.000Z, `to` 2299-12-31T23:59:59.999Z, exclusive) returns to the same caller, within its scope for a scoped key or viewer token, or null when that search finds none. It describes what is stored now, not what ever existed: an empty history before it does not prove that nothing happened then. `retentionDays` is the project's configured retention policy, the same for every reader of the project, and the one value here that a scoped caller could not already find. Retention runs (hourly, and right after the policy is shortened) delete older events for good; the policy is not a bound on what search returns, since older events can still be stored and found between runs (for example one that arrived dated in the past). So `oldestEventAt` can lie before now minus `retentionDays`, and it can move back as well as forward. Raising `retentionDays` restores nothing. To read a whole history, search from `oldestEventAt` to the end of the searchable range, `to` 2299-12-31T23:59:59.999Z (exclusive): an event can be dated up to one day after the server received it, so a `to` computed from your own clock can miss events.

schema.description: How far back the caller can read. To read a whole history, search from `oldestEventAt` to `to` 2299-12-31T23:59:59.999Z, the end of the searchable range (an event can be dated up to one day after the server received it, so a `to` from your own clock can miss events), and do not take an empty answer before `oldestEventAt` as proof that nothing happened.

oldestEventAt.description: The `timestamp` of the oldest event this caller can find through search (ISO 8601 UTC, milliseconds): the first event of an `order=asc` search over the widest window, or null when that search finds none. It describes what is stored now: retention or deletion may have removed older events, raising `retentionDays` brings none back, and it can move back as well as forward (an event can arrive dated in the past).

retentionDays.description: The project's configured retention policy in days, the same for every reader of the project. Retention runs (hourly, and right after the policy is shortened) delete older events for good. It is a policy, not a bound on what a search returns: between runs, older events can still be stored and found.

mask.description: Field masks applied to every returned event. `ip` and `user_agent` empty `context.ip` and `context.userAgent`. `actor_email` shows `actor.email`, the impersonator email attribute `impersonator.email` and an actor or impersonator name that carries an address (contains `@` or a compatibility form of it, equals the email, or is 511 UTF-16 units or longer) as `masked:<24 hex>` pseudonyms, stable per project (impersonator pseudonyms are keyed by role, so they do not match the actor pseudonym of the same address), and removes attribute paths below `impersonator.email`. Every protected attribute path below covers the paths below it too, which are removed from events, and matches attribute keys in any ASCII letter case (`impersonator.Email`). A masked scope cannot filter or facet on what its masks hide (422 `invalid_query`, reason `not_allowed`): for `ip` the `ip` field and the `context.ip` attribute; for `user_agent` the `context.userAgent` attribute; for `actor_email` the `actor.email` field and attribute, the literal `actor.name` and `impersonator.name` attributes (removed from events too), and the `impersonator.email` attribute (as a facet, `field=attr.impersonator.email`). Other names stay readable: `actor.name` and `impersonator.name` filters read an address-carrying name as empty, and facets on `actor.name`, `actor`, `impersonator` and `impersonator.name` show an address-carrying name (as a value or label) as its pseudonym. Any mask drops the original payload. See docs/scoped-read-access.md#masks.
